issues.issue: The statement that a withdrawal reduces the Death Benefit by reducing "the Policy Value if Option B is in effect" sits against Section 15, which spells out that under Option B the withdrawal comes out of Policy Value and "the Total Face Amount does not change". The two descriptions of the same event are stated at different levels and could be read to differ.

The insurer may cut back the Minimum Death Benefit where the Net Amount at Risk "exceeds our guidelines and limitations that may be in effect", a standard that is nowhere defined or disclosed in the policy. The insured cannot tell from the contract when the reduction right arises.

Section 8 provides that on the Age 100 Anniversary an Option B policy changes to Option A, "which means the Total Face Amount will not be increased by the Policy Value" — the opposite of the rule stated here for a B-to-A change. The exception and the general rule point in different directions.

This says a reduction in Total Face Amount occurs "with no change to the surrender charge schedule", while Section 5 requires a pro-rata Surrender Charge to be deducted on any reduction in Total Face Amount. The two treatments of the same event conflict.

The second sentence — "You are limited to one surrender charges for this policy" — is missing its object (evidently "change in Death Benefit Option per Policy Year") and is ungrammatical, so the limitation it imposes cannot be read off the words. As written it states no intelligible restriction.

The test compares "total premiums paid by you less partial withdrawals, since policy issue, less policy debt" against cumulative Monthly Guarantee Premiums, but the placement of "since policy issue" and the deduction of policy debt leave the computation open to more than one reading. Whether accrued loan interest reduces the test amount is not clear.

The clause says that on a change in face amount, rider or risk classification "we will modify the Monthly Guarantee Premium" without stating any basis, formula or limit for the modification. The revised figure that determines the no-lapse guarantee is left to the insurer's unstated method.

Section 6 provides that on a "Change from Option B to Option A: the Total Face Amount will be increased by the Policy Value", whereas this bullet says the same change at Age 100 means "the Total Face Amount will not be increased by the Policy Value". The two provisions state opposite consequences for the same conversion.

The post-100 Death Benefit is the greater of Total Face Amount or Policy Value, which omits the Section 6 Minimum Death Benefit (Policy Value times the applicable percentage) that the opening words of Section 8 say continues to apply "except as follows". Whether the Minimum Death Benefit survives after Age 100 is unsettled.

The flat statement that after the Age 100 Anniversary "we will not accept any further premium payments" cannot be squared with Section 4's promise that "in no event ... will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating", given that Section 8 keeps the default rules alive after Age 100.

Default here is cured under Section 11 by "payment of additional premiums or repayment of policy debt", but the immediately preceding paragraph of Section 8 bars any further premium payments after Age 100. The cure mechanism is partly unavailable in the very period this paragraph governs.

Component (d) charges for "any applicable Additional Ratings shown in Section 1", but Section 1 records "Additional Ratings Not Applicable" while classifying the Insured as 150% substandard. Where the substandard loading is charged is left unexplained.

The clause states that cost of insurance rates "are based on" an enumerated list of factors (sex, Age, Risk Classification, face amounts, Net Amount at Risk and duration), leaving open whether that list is exhaustive and whether rates may reflect factors not listed. "Based on" does not say whether the listed items are the only permissible inputs.

This list of rate factors, fixed "as of the Policy Date", stands against the Section 1 footnote asserting a right to "change ... the amount of cost of insurance deducted" and against the redetermination paragraph later in Section 9. Which controls a later rate increase is contestable.

"[S]uch rates will be based on our expectations of future mortality, persistency, investment earnings, expense experience, capital and reserve requirements, and tax assumptions" enumerates permitted factors without saying whether the list is exhaustive or whether every listed factor must actually change. "Based on our expectations" is also open to reading either as a substantive constraint or as a mere description.

This constraint on the rate basis is in tension with the Section 1 Table of Values footnote, which states flatly that "We have the right to change ... the amount of cost of insurance deducted under the policy" with no stated limitation. Whether the footnote qualifies the Section 9 limits is a genuine question.

"[A]ny adjustment for the Minimum Death Benefit" is not identified or quantified anywhere, and the Net Amount at Risk formula that follows already builds in the Minimum Death Benefit Percentage. The sentence's operative content is uncertain.

The redetermination power is limited only by a requirement that it be "on a basis that does not discriminate unfairly within any class of insureds", where neither "discriminate unfairly" nor "class of insureds" is defined. Whether the insurer may single out a subgroup within a rate class turns entirely on those words.

The unqualified permission to "re-determine Cost of Insurance rates" must be read with the preceding sentence limiting rates to the insurer's expectations of the enumerated factors and with the Section 1 footnote asserting an unrestricted right to change charges. The three passages give different accounts of the same power.

The formula subtracts (a) from the greater of (b) or (c), but (c) is itself defined as (a) multiplied by the Minimum Death Benefit Percentage, and limb (b) is set out in a garbled clause covering both Death Benefit Options at once. The arithmetic that produces the Net Amount at Risk is not unambiguously stated.

The interest-crediting sentence is broken mid-way, so the words tying the credited rate to the insurer's "anticipation of future investment earnings, mortality, persistency, expense and administrative costs, and taxes" have no grammatical subject; that standard then sits beside "We may, in our sole discretion, change the interest rate(s)." Whether crediting is constrained by the listed anticipations or purely discretionary is left open.

The rate table is internally garbled: the second band gives "50%" as an Additional Interest Rate (evidently 0.50%), and the columns are labelled so that a higher credited rate on unloaned Policy Value produces the larger bonus. The Additional Interest actually payable cannot be computed with confidence from the table as printed.

This exception is numbered "(i)", the same numeral as the preceding exception, so the two items in the list are not distinguished. The mislabelling obscures which exception a cross-reference to "(i)" picks up.

The refusal to process any premium that would disqualify the policy as a life insurance contract contradicts Section 4's promise that "in no event, however, will we refuse to accept any premium necessary to prevent the policy from terminating." A premium can fall within both descriptions.

The middle of the paragraph is broken ("Unless we agree oth === are subject to the Maximum Annual Premium sho ... Overloan Protection, no further premiums may be paid once Overlo: goes into effect"), so the qualification on the right to pay additional premiums and the Maximum Annual Premium limit cannot be read as written. The operative restriction is missing words.

The reserved right to "limit the number and amount of premium payments in any Policy Year" cuts against the same section's grant that "you may pay additional premiums at any time" and against Section 4's promise never to refuse a premium necessary to prevent termination. The extent of the insurer's veto over premiums is not settled.

The notice must be sent "at least 15 days and not more than 45 days prior to termination of coverage", which does not fit the 61-day grace period running from the date of default that the same section prescribes. When the notice obligation is triggered is left to inference.

The paragraph is missing its operative opening — the words granting the election and stating what the policy is "lapsed to" are gone — so the benefit's trigger and content cannot be read from the text. What survives is only the calculation basis for a benefit whose availability is unstated.

A reduced paid-up option is not among the outcomes recognised by Section 12, which says the policy "will terminate automatically" when the grace period expires, and the feature appears nowhere in the Table of Contents. The two provisions describe different fates for a lapsing policy.

The list of three automatic termination events is presented as exhaustive, yet Section 11 contemplates a Reduced Paid-Up Benefit on lapse and Section 14 keeps a policy in force through Overloan Protection. Whether the list truly accounts for every way coverage ends is open.

The paragraph begins mid-sentence ("request. A loan may not be taken after you have exercised Overloan Protecti"), so the sentence actually granting the right to borrow and stating its conditions is absent. The scope of the loan right must be supplied from outside the words.

The proviso that the Maximum Loan Value "will not be less than the Preferred Loan Amount plus accrued interest ... but in no event greater than the current Policy Value" can push the figure above limb (b), the current Surrender Value, contradicting the "lesser of (a) or (b)" rule in the same paragraph. Which cap governs is not stated.

The first sentence is truncated ("Loan interest will accrue on a daily basis from the date of"), leaving the accrual start date unstated. The rest of the paragraph presupposes a rule the text no longer contains.

"[A] change in the Interest Rate" is capitalised but undefined, and the sentence sits in the loan-interest paragraph, so it may mean the credited interest rate under Section 9 or the policy loan interest rate. Which rate triggers the anti-lapse protection is genuinely uncertain.

This anti-lapse promise has to be reconciled with Section 11, which makes default turn mechanically on whether Monthly Deductions exceed the Net Policy Value or Net Surrender Value regardless of cause. A rate change that produces such a shortfall engages both provisions.
